extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal scholars, and practitioners interested in English constitutional and international law (Blackstone's Commentaries)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository treatment of the crown's prerogatives in foreign and domestic affairs, including diplomatic immunities, treaty and war powers, military authority, judicial prerogatives, proclamations, and related statutory limits. Intended as a doctrinal reference and teaching text on the scope and limits of executive authority under English law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerogative as discretionary public power (Locke)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prerogative consists in the discretionary power of acting for the public good, where the positive laws are silent; if that discretionary power be abused to the public detriment, such prerogative is exerted in an unconstitutional manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When prerogative acts manifestly cause grievance or dishonour to the kingdom, parliament may call the king's advisers to account (e.g., by impeachment). The text treats the prerogative as bounded by public good and susceptible to parliamentary check when abused.

rubrics_metrics.name: King as representative in foreign affairs; sole power over ambassadors
rubrics_metrics.description: The king, as delegate or representative of his people, has the sole power of sending ambassadors to foreign states and receiving ambassadors at home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What the king does in relation to foreign powers is treated as the act of the whole nation; acts without the king's concurrence are acts of private men and not binding on the nation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambassadors' status governed by law of nations, not municipal law
rubrics_metrics.description: The rights, powers, duties, and privileges of ambassadors are determined by the law of nature and nations, and not by any municipal constitutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because ambassadors represent foreign sovereigns, they ought not to be subject to the mere municipal laws of the host state; if they offend, they should be recalled and dealt with by their own sovereign. This is a general principle of diplomatic immunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of diplomatic immunity (mala prohibita vs mala in se)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is dispute whether exemption of ambassadors extends to all crimes (natural and positive) or only to mala prohibita (e.g., coining) and not to mala in se (e.g., murder); historical English law sometimes restricted immunity for crimes against natural law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone notes earlier authorities held ambassadors privileged but liable for offences against the law of reason and nature; modern European practice generally favors broader immunity, with few recent examples of punishment even for atrocious offences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambassador criminal liability for treason against sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: If an ambassador conspires the death of the king in whose land he is, he may be condemned and executed for treason; for other species of treason the practice may differ and the ambassador is usually sent to his own kingdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This position is presented as historically recognized and grounded in the idea that ambassadors remain subject to the primary law of nature where municipal law annexes punishment to natural crimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil immunity of ambassadors and statutory protection (7 Ann. c.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: In respect to civil suits, ambassadors and their train cannot be prosecuted for debt or contract in the courts of the kingdom; after the 1708 arrest of a Muscovite ambassador, Parliament enacted statute 7 Ann. c.12 to enforce such privileges and nullify process arresting ambassadors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: traders within the bankrupt laws who are in service of an ambassador are not privileged; ambassador's servants must be registered with the secretary of state (and transmitted to sheriffs) to be protected from arrest. Persons prosecuting or executing process against ambassadors are deemed violators of the law of nations and punishable as the law officers see fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: King's prerogative to make treaties, leagues, and alliances
rubrics_metrics.description: It is by the law of nations essential to the goodness of a league that it be made by the sovereign power; in England that sovereign power quoad hoc is vested in the person of the king.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treaties made by the king bind the whole community and cannot be legally annulled by other powers; parliamentary impeachment serves as a constitutional check on ministers advising or concluding treaties detrimental to the nation's honour or interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sole prerogative to make war and peace
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of making war and peace is vested in the sovereign; private persons' hostilities do not bind the state and are treated as piracy or robbery unless publicly undertaken by the sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grotius's rationale: denunciation of war precedes hostilities so that war is clearly by the will of the whole community. In England war must be publicly declared and proclaimed by the king to be binding. Parliamentary impeachment provides a restraint on ministers who improperly begin, conduct, or conclude wars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters of marque and reprisal (prerogative and statutory form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters of marque and reprisal are grantable by the law of nations whenever subjects are oppressed by foreigners and justice is denied; they are a species of prerogative nearly related to the power of making war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute 4 Hen. V. c.7 prescribes form: sufferer applies to lord privy-seal for letters of request under privy seal; if no satisfaction, lord chancellor issues letters of marque under the great seal, permitting seizure of aggressor nation's property until satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to grant safe-conducts and regulate admission of strangers
rubrics_metrics.description: The prerogative of granting safe-conducts is vested in the king; by law of nations no member of one society has a right to intrude into another without such admission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safe-conducts (particularly in older statutes) must be granted under the great seal and enrolled in chancery to be effective. Foreigners in distress or those who behave peaceably while their nation is at peace are under king's protection but may be sent home at the king's pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magna Carta protection for foreign merchants
rubrics_metrics.description: By Magna Carta all merchants (unless publicly prohibited beforehand) shall have safe conduct to depart from, to come into, to tarry in, and to go through England for the exercise of merchandize, without unreasonable imposts, except in time of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If war breaks out merchants of the enemy nation may be attached (detained) without harm to person or goods until reciprocal treatment of English merchants is ascertained; this is an early statutory protection of foreign commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: King as constituent of supreme legislative power and veto/rejection prerogative
rubrics_metrics.description: The king is a constituent part of the supreme legislative power and has the prerogative of rejecting provisions in parliament which he judges improper to be passed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The king is not bound by any act of parliament unless he is named therein by special and particular words; however, acts expressly for preservation of public rights and suppression of public wrongs that do not interfere with established rights of the crown are binding. The king may avail himself of acts even if not specially named.

rubrics_metrics.name: King as generalissimo: sole power over raising/regulating forces and fortifications
rubrics_metrics.description: The king, as first in military command, has the sole power of raising and regulating fleets and armies, and erecting, manning, and governing forts and places of strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute 13 Car. II. c.6 declares the sole supreme government and command of the militia and all forces to be the undoubted right of the king. No subject may build castles or defensible fortresses without royal licence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to prohibit export of arms and control subjects' travel
rubrics_metrics.description: By statutes (12 Car. II. c.4 and 29 Geo. II. c.16) the king may prohibit exportation of arms or ammunition; by common law the king may confine subjects to the realm or recall them (writs such as ne exeat regnum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disobeying a royal writ to stay or return may result in seizure of lands until return and liability to fines and imprisonment. Historical statutory and common-law mechanisms enforce military and security prerogatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: King as fountain of justice and conservator of the peace
rubrics_metrics.description: The king is the distributor (fountain) of justice and general conservator of the peace; he has the right of erecting courts of judicature, and judicial jurisdictions run generally in the king's name and under his seal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The original power of judicature is lodged in society but delegated to magistrates; courts and jurisdictions are mediately or immediately derived from the crown, and judges execute justice in the king's name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security and independence of judges (tenure and salary protections)
rubrics_metrics.description: To maintain dignity and independence of judges, commissions are to be during good behaviour (not at pleasure) and their salaries ascertained and established; removal allowed only on address of both houses of parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute 13 W. III. c.2 changed commissions from durante bene placito to quamdiu bene se gesserint; statute 1 Geo. III. c.23 continued judges during good behaviour notwithstanding demise of the crown and secured full salaries during commission continuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: King as prosecutor in criminal prosecutions; nature of offences
rubrics_metrics.description: In criminal proceedings the king appears in the capacity of prosecutor; offences are either against the king's peace or his crown and dignity and are laid as such in indictments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because prosecutions are in the king's name (the public delegated to a visible magistrate), the king is the proper person to prosecute public offences. The king's pardoning power does not extend to parliamentary impeachments, where the commons are prosecutors in their own names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proclamations: binding only when enforcing existing law, not creating new law
rubrics_metrics.description: Royal proclamations are binding upon subjects when they are grounded upon and enforce the laws of the realm; proclamations that contradict old laws or establish new ones (assume dispensing or legislative power) will not bind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: proclamation forbidding leaving the realm for three weeks as embargo in time of war may be binding if founded on prior law; but proclamation disarming protestants or allowing papists arms in contradiction to statute would be invalid. Statute 31 Hen. VIII. c.8 once attempted to make proclamations have force of acts of parliament but was repealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: King as fountain of honour, office, and privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: The king is the fountain of honour, of office, and of privilege; in this sense he is the parent (not merely distributor) of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prerogative is distinct from the fountain of justice: here the king truly originates honours, offices, and privileges rather than merely dispensing an existing public right.
